Hebrew has no relative adverb: 'asher ... sham' is the locative relative construction, and the ASV spends one English word, 'where', on it, so the whole expression is one unit headed on the morpheme carrying the locative lexeme (rule 30, whose 'wherein' is the same relative-plus-resumptive idiom, and rule 35's 'kol asher' -> 'whatsoever'). The intervening verb keeps its own unit. Reading 'sham' as a resumptive element left unrepresented under rule 22 remains defensible, but rule 22 governs a repetition of the same element, not the parts of an idiom.
The inflected verb takes its English subject pronoun and the periphrastic 'was to' with the lexical verb as head (rule 17).

variant_decisions.evidence: Qere הַשְּׂבָכָה carries the article, the ketiv שבכה does not. The ASV's 'beside the network' supplies an English definite article that anaphoric reference to the network of v.17-18 would require under either reading, so the wording does not distinguish them; the qere base stands.

variant_decisions.evidence: Qere וְקָו and ketiv וקוה are orthographic variants of the same noun קָו 'line', both rendered 'and a line'. Nothing in the ASV wording or its notes distinguishes them; the qere base stands.

The ASV recasts the verbless clause so that the demonstrative is the predicate: "was on this manner". Rule 20 gives the supplied copula to the predicate's unit, and "on"/"manner" are the connective and the generic noun the ASV supplies to expand the demonstrative, so the head is "this".

Possessive לְ recast as English "have": the preposition is what makes the verbless clause possessive, so "had" realizes it rather than being left unrepresented. Reading "they had" as one unit on the suffix, with לָ unrepresented under rule 40, remains defensible.
The suffix takes the subject pronoun the recasting gives it (rule 40's range).

Verbless existential clause: the supplied "there were" joins the predicate that licenses it (rules 20-21), which is the בֵּין phrase, with the dummy subject inside that unit. Attaching "there were" to the subject מִסְגְּרֹת instead is defensible.
